Black Watch
description:
Also known as the "government sett", Black Watch tartan was first worn by the six independent companies raised by General George Wade to police the Scottish highlanders in 1725. Although the origins of the tartan are unknown, the dark blue and green colours are believed to have been worn by all six original companies, albeit in varying patterns.

Today the Black Watch is the 3rd Battalion, Royal Regiment of Scotland. Traditionally the Black Watch tartan can be worn by anyone without a tartan of their own.

name: Brim-DeForest of Balvaird Castle
description: Based on the 1842 Johnston tartan from the Vestiarium Scoticum to represent the Brim-DeForest's ancestral links to the Johnston Clan. The tartan was designed for the first of the name Brim-DeForest: Brady Brim-DeForest of Balvaird Castle. The tartan is for use by all members of the Brim-DeForest family and those that bear the surname. To mark the great interest in cartography of Brim-DeForest of Balvaird, the dark red squares comprise 56 threads - the northern latitude of the family seat at Balvaird Castle in Perthshire. Its longitude west is represented by the three gold lines on that same red. The ancient DeForest connection with France is shown by the French flag - the Tricolour - whose colours are also in the Brim-DeForest coat of arms (with gold) and the Stars and Stripes of the Brim-DeForest’s home country. The thin pink lines are for Brady and Jessica's daughter, Hypatia.

Fogarty (Tipperary)
description: Blue and gold are the primary colours of the Fogarty crest. They also signify the tie between the Fogarty Clan and County Tipperary whose crest has the same colours. The green and brown are a link to the Tara tartan, with Tara representing the ancient kings of Ireland and Fogarty representing the ancient kings of Ely. The green and brown also represent the fertile landscape of Eliogarty which will link the tartan to the wheat sheaf on the family crest. The red, white and black accents are found in both the Tara and Tipperary County Crest tartans: the red represents the blood of Fogartys shed in battle, not only in ancient Ireland but for those who have served as warriors throughout history. This links to the heraldic lions on the family crest representing the great warriors and chiefs who have carried the name Fogarty into battle. The white represents the white crescent found on the family crest representing hope of glory.

description: Based on Hamilton tartan in honour of Alexander Hamilton, first US Secretary of the Treasury and founder of the US Coast Guard. The blue is changed to modern Coast Guard Blue symbolic of the seas and skies where the men and women of the Coast Guard work. The red represents the courage and sacrifice of Coast Guard members in peace and in war. The ten thread count white overstripe is a symbol of the white sails of the first ten cutters of the service authorised by Hamilton.

name: Veitch H & Family
description: The colours chosen for this tartan are intended to represent the history of the Veitch surname which was first recorded in Berwickshire when Randolph Veitch witnessed a charter by Henry de Graham c.1200; red and grey represent the Aberdeenshire granite of Darwyk House, first built by the Veitch family; green represents the Dawyck arboretum and botanical gardens; blue represents the River Tweed and the Scrape burn which runs through the gardens; yellow and white represent the yellow Winter Aconites and white Snowdrops which carpet the banks of the Scarpe burn in springtime.

name: Victoria State (Australia)
description: Designed in November 1998 by Betty Johnston of House of Tartan in Canberra, Australia. The blue is that of the Eureka Stockade Flag and the pink is the colour of the State's floral emblem the Pink Heath flower. 'We swear by the Southern Cross to stand truly by each other and fight to defend our rights and liberties.' Beneath the starry flag of rebellion, that oath was taken by hundreds of gold diggers at Ballarat in 1854. The Eureka rebellion led by Peter Lalor was a short lived revolt against petty officialdom and although a military failure, led to political and personal benefits for many Australians.
